passage:
Monday. Lalit's message came at eleven at night: "Bhai, can you send some for the trip? Also, science elective or commerce?" It was the third money request that month. Chaitanya sent it, then lay awake, feeling used, and guilty for feeling it.

Saturday, two weeks later. When Lalit asked again, Chaitanya called instead of transferring. "I'll help with the trip once. But you choose the elective. What did you enjoy in class?" Lalit stammered, then talked for ten minutes about his physics teacher. "Sounds like you already know," Chaitanya said.

Sunday, a month after that. Lalit sent a photo of his first earnings from the bookshop. "Bought my own textbooks. Still want advice on one thing 🙂" Chaitanya smiled and typed, "Ask."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy with his own earnings?
How did Chaitanya feel after sending the money on Monday?
qa.a: Used, and also guilty for feeling used.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya change on Saturday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Chaitanya called instead of transferring, helped once, and asked Lalit to make the elective choice. A month later Lalit was earning and buying his own textbooks.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when asked to choose the elective himself?
qa.a: Nervous, since he stammered at first. But talking about his physics teacher shows that being trusted helped him find his own answer.

grounding: A younger sibling leans on Chaitanya for money and decisions; Chaitanya supports kindly while encouraging his independence, across three days.

passage:
Dear Sabina,
I'm writing because every call between us lately has turned into a request, and I don't want to say something sharp on the phone.
This month you asked me to choose your elective, decide whether to leave your PG, and send 3,000 for the trip. I did all three. I've been doing this since you started college, and I'm glad to help. But I've noticed I feel used after our calls, and I don't think that's good for either of us.
Here's what I'd like: for decisions, tell me what you think first, then I'll share my view. You're good at thinking things through; you just don't trust it yet. For money, I'll help with college emergencies, but not trips. Maybe look into the tutoring job your warden mentioned?
I love you. I'll always be your safety net. I just don't want to be your only one.
Your didi,
Usha

qa.q: How much did Sabina ask for the trip?
How does Usha feel after their calls?
qa.a: Usha feels used after the calls, even while glad to help.

qa.q: What does Usha propose to build Sabina's independence?
qa.a: Sabina shares a view first on decisions, and Usha helps with college emergencies but not trips, pointing to the tutoring job.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Stung and a little embarrassed at first, but also trusted, since Usha says Sabina is good at thinking things through.

grounding: Shows a younger sibling leaning on you for money and decisions, and supporting kindly while encouraging independence instead of rescuing repeatedly.

passage:
Honestly, Rina, I think I created the problem with Neelam myself.
She's my little sister. When she failed her driving test, I booked the retest. When her landlord raised the rent, I called him. When she couldn't decide between two jobs, I picked one. Every time she panicked, I swooped in. And then I'd hang up furious, thinking, why can't she do anything herself?
Last week she called at eleven at night: "Didi, my laptop crashed before my submission, what do I do?" I opened my mouth to say I'd call the repair shop, and stopped.
I said, "What are your options?" Silence. Then she listed three: borrow her roommate's laptop, email the professor, use the college lab in the morning. I said, "Which one first?" She chose. Submitted by midnight.
She called back just to say, "I did it." She sounded so proud.
So that's me, Devika, retired rescuer. Mostly retired.

qa.q: How did Devika feel after rescuing Neelam each time?
qa.a: Furious and used, wondering why Neelam couldn't do anything herself.

qa.q: What did Devika do differently at eleven that night?
qa.a: Asked "What are your options?" and "Which one first?", letting Neelam choose and solve it herself.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel after submitting by midnight?
qa.a: Proud; she called back just to say "I did it."

grounding: Illustrates rescuing a dependent younger sibling until it feels like being used, then supporting her in a way that builds independence.
